\[

\[
\|\nabla h\|_2^2\geq c_K\|h\|_2^4
 \log\bigl(e+\|h\|_2^2\bigr)-C_K.                 \tag{1}
\]
Here \(H^{-1}\) is the inhomogeneous Sobolev space.

For completeness, positivity is what supplies the logarithm. The kernel of \((1-\Delta)^{-1}\) is positive and behaves like \(\log(1/|x|)\) near zero. Consequently,
\[
\iint_{|x-y|\leq r}h(x)h(y)\,dx\,dy
 \leq \frac{C_K}{\log(1/r)}.
\]
For a nonnegative smooth compactly supported mollifier \(\rho_r\), this implies
\[
\|\rho_r*h\|_2^2\leq \frac{C_K}{r^2\log(1/r)}.
\]
Combining this with
\[
\|h-\rho_r*h\|_2^2\leq Cr^2\|\nabla h\|_2^2

Split the vorticity by solving the linear transport–diffusion equation with the actual velocity:

g^\nu(0)=\mu_0^\nu,\quad f^\nu(0)=f_0^\nu.

The standard scalar estimates give
\[
g^\nu\geq0,\qquad
\|g^\nu(t)\|_1\leq 2M,\qquad
\|f^\nu(t)\|_1+\|f^\nu(t)\|_p\leq M.
\]
These statements, including the splitting for measure initial data, follow by approximation.

Since \(L^1\cap L^p\hookrightarrow H^{-1}\) in dimension two for every \(p>1\), the velocity energy bound yields
\[

\leq \|\omega^\nu(t)\|_{H^{-1}}+\|f^\nu(t)\|_{H^{-1}}
\leq C_{p,M}.
\]
Apply (1) to \(g^\nu\). Its scalar energy identity, with

\[
Y'(t)\leq-c_{p,M}\nu Y(t)^2\log(e+Y(t))+C_{p,M}\nu.
\]

\[

\qquad \tfrac12\leq t\leq1,                       \tag{2}

for sufficiently small \(\nu\).

\[
\mu^\nu\ge0,\qquad \|\mu^\nu\|_1+\|f^\nu\|_1+\|f^\nu\|_p\le C.
\]
All constants below may depend on \(p,M\), but not on \(\nu\).

\[
\|\mu^\nu(t)\|_{H^{-1}}
\le \|\operatorname{curl}u^\nu(t)\|_{H^{-1}}
+\|f^\nu(t)\|_{H^{-1}}\le C.
\]
The kernel of \((1-\Delta)^{-1}\) is positive and behaves like \(\log(1/|x|)\) near zero. Consequently,
\[
\iint_{|x-y|<r}d\mu^\nu(t,x)\,d\mu^\nu(t,y)
\le \frac{C}{\log(1/r)},\qquad 0<r<\tfrac14. \tag{1}
\]
This holds on both domains.

Here is the resulting logarithmic Nash estimate. For any nonnegative \(g\) with the preceding mass and \(H^{-1}\) bounds, Gaussian smoothing and (1) give
\[
\|e^{\Delta/R^2}g\|_2^2\le \frac{CR^2}{\log R},\qquad R\ge4.
\]
Indeed, split its positive Gaussian kernel at distance \(R^{-1/2}\), using (1) inside and Gaussian decay outside. A frequency decomposition therefore yields
\[
\|g\|_2^2\le \frac{CR^2}{\log R}
+\frac{C}{R^2}\|\nabla g\|_2^2.
\]
Optimizing in \(R\), for sufficiently large \(\|g\|_2\),
\[
\|\nabla g\|_2^2
\ge c\|g\|_2^4\log\!\bigl(e+\|g\|_2^2\bigr).
\]

Apply this to \(\mu^\nu(t)\). Its enstrophy identity, followed by integration of the resulting differential inequality, gives
\[
\|\mu^\nu(t)\|_2^2
\le C+\frac{C}{\nu t\log(1/(\nu t))}
\]
when \(\nu t\) is small. These estimates can first be applied to regularized data and then passed to measure data.

For the other component, divergence-free advection–diffusion smoothing gives, on \(1/2\le t\le1\),
\[
\nu\|f^\nu(t)\|_2^2
\le C\nu^{\min\{1,\,2-2/p\}}.
\]
Thus
\[
D_\nu
\le 2\nu\int_{1/2}^1
\bigl(\|\mu^\nu(t)\|_2^2+\|f^\nu(t)\|_2^2\bigr)\,dt
\le \frac{C}{\log(1/\nu)}.
\]

\[

 \leq \frac{C K^2}{\log(1/r)}.
\]
If \(g_r\) is a compactly supported mollification at scale \(r\), this implies
\[
\|g_r\|_2^2\leq \frac{C K^2}{r^2\log(1/r)}.
\]

\[
\|g\|_2^2\leq C r^2\|\nabla g\|_2^2+2\|g_r\|_2^2,
\]

### Upper bound

We first describe two elementary encoding constructions.

**Coarse localization.** If \(\operatorname{Var}(X)\le1\) and \(|\mu|\le M\), nonadaptive one-bit queries can produce \(c\) satisfying
\[
|c-\mu|\le C
\]
with failure probability at most \(\delta\), using \(O(\log(M+2)+\log(1/\delta))\) samples.

Here is one construction. Partition the line into bins of a sufficiently large constant width, and use three shifted partitions. For each partition, assign independent public random binary codewords to its bins; sample \(i\) transmits coordinate \(i\) of its bin's codeword. In at least one partition, the mean is well inside a bin, so Chebyshev's inequality makes the transmitted bits a small-noise version of that bin's codeword. Hamming-distance decoding, a Chernoff bound, and a union bound over the \(O(M+1)\) relevant bins give the assertion. The same bounds exclude acceptance of bins far from the mean in the other partitions.

For \(M=e^{t^2}\) and \(\delta\asymp t^{-1}\), this costs \(O(t^2)\) samples.

**Fine estimation after localization.** The queries in the following construction are all specified in advance; only their interpretation uses \(c\).

Take dyadic spacings from \(h\asymp t^{-1}\) to \(R\asymp t\), a total of
\[
K=O(\log t)
\]
levels. At each spacing \(r\), make available quantizers on three shifted grids. After learning \(c\), select a grid whose boundaries are at distance at least a constant multiple of \(r\) from \(c\). Write its quantizer as \(Q_r\).

For successive levels, the increment
\[
A_r(x)=Q_r(x)-Q_{2r}(x)
\]
has only a constant number of possible values and is periodic. Consequently it can be encoded by a constant number of one-bit indicator queries. All possible choices of the two shifted grids are included in advance, at constant overhead.

After subtracting \(A_r(c)\), each selected increment is zero when \(|x-c|<a r\), and has magnitude at most \(Cr\). Thus
\[
\sum_r\mathbb E\bigl[(A_r(X)-A_r(c))^2\bigr]
 \le C\mathbb E[(X-c)^2]\le C
\]
on the localization event. Allocating equally many samples to the levels therefore gives an unbiased estimate of the telescoping sum with variance \(O(K/m)\), where \(m\) is the total number of samples in one estimation block.

The bottom quantization error is \(O(h)\). At the top, replacing \(Q_R(X)\) by \(Q_R(c)\) introduces bias at most
\[
C\,\mathbb E\!\left[|X-c|\mathbf1_{\{|X-c|\ge aR\}}\right]
 \le \frac{C\mathbb E[(X-c)^2]}R.
\]
Choosing the constants in \(h\) and \(R\) makes the total bias at most \(1/(4t)\).

Hence \(m=O(t^2K)\) gives constant success probability. Taking the median of \(O(\log t)\) independent blocks reduces the failure probability to \(O(t^{-1})\). Including localization,
\[
N(t)\le C t^2(\log t)^2.
\]
All grids, indicators, and code queries are Borel measurable and nonadaptive.

C\log(2/h)\bigl(1+\mathbb E(X-\mathbb EX)^2\bigr).

The relevant representation obstruction is the following standard result:
> If a free Heyting algebra on finitely many generators is isomorphic to the Heyting algebra of subterminals of an elementary topos, then it is complete.

For \(n=0\), the free algebra is the two-element algebra, realized by \(\operatorname{Sub}_{\mathbf{Set}}(1)\).

For \(n=1\), the free algebra is the Rieger–Nishimura algebra. Its lattice consists of the familiar ascending ladder, together with its top: every infinite subset has supremum \(1\), and all remaining suprema exist. Thus it is a complete Heyting algebra, hence a frame. The localic sheaf topos on this frame has precisely \(F_1\) as its algebra of subterminals.

In contrast, the free Heyting algebra \(F_2\) is not complete. The representation obstruction therefore rules out an elementary topos with subterminal algebra \(F_2\). This is the first failure.

We use two standard facts about arithmetic spin lattices of type \(B_n\), \(n\ge2\), in the higher-\(S\)-rank setting here:
* their congruence kernels are finite, and their profinite completions determine the finite local fields and local spin groups, up to permutation;
* if their finite adelic spin groups are isomorphic, they have finite-index subgroups with isomorphic profinite completions.

For the second assertion, finite congruence kernels cause no problem: choose open subgroups of the completions avoiding those kernels, then intersect their images in the common finite adelic group.

### The parity obstruction

An odd-dimensional quadratic form has a unique representative, up to isometry, in its similarity class whose determinant is \(1\) modulo squares. Use this normalization throughout. At a real place, the Hasse invariant of a form with \(b\) negative directions is
\[
(-1)^{b(b-1)/2}.
\]
Consequently, the normalized real forms in question have invariants
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c}
\text{real spin group}&\text{normalized negative index}&\text{Hasse invariant}\\ \hline
\operatorname{Spin}(2n-1,2)&2&-1\\
\operatorname{Spin}(2n,1)&2n&(-1)^n\\
\text{compact}&0&1.
\end{array}
\]

Suppose the two lattices have isomorphic profinite completions. Finite-local rigidity identifies their normalized quadratic forms at the finite places, allowing a permutation of places and possibly different number fields. Thus their products of finite Hasse invariants agree. Hilbert reciprocity then forces their products of real Hasse invariants to agree:
\[
(-1)^r=(-1)^{nr}.
\]
Hence a necessary condition is
\[
r(n-1)\equiv0\pmod2.
\]
In particular, when \(r\) is odd, \(n=2\) is impossible.

Conversely, suppose \(r(n-1)\) is even. Choose a totally real field with more than \(r\) real places. Prescribe two determinant-one forms of dimension \(2n+1\), with:
* the two required signatures at the same \(r\) real places;
* positive-definite signatures at every remaining real place;
* identical isometry classes at all finite places.

The displayed parity condition is exactly the compatibility condition for the two real Hasse products. The existence theorem for quadratic forms over number fields therefore supplies such forms. The definite real place makes both forms anisotropic over the number field, so their arithmetic lattices are cocompact. Strong approximation gives irreducibility.

Their finite adelic spin groups agree. The congruence-kernel facts above therefore give finite-index lattices with isomorphic profinite completions. Passing to corresponding further finite-index subgroups makes both torsion-free. They are finitely presented and residually finite.

and its torsion-free compact quotient is Kähler.

The second is not Kähler, by the standard harmonic-map obstruction for irreducible cocompact lattices in products of real hyperbolic spaces of dimension at least \(3\). Here each hyperbolic factor has dimension \(2n\ge4\).

Thus \(n=2\) works for even \(r\), while for odd \(r\) the obstruction excludes \(2\) and the construction works for \(3\).

The answer depends only on the parity of \(r\).

We use two standard consequences of the congruence subgroup and rigidity theorems for spin groups of type \(B_n\), \(n\ge2\), with total real rank at least two:

* Their cocompact arithmetic lattices have finite congruence kernel. Consequently, lattices with isomorphic finite adelic groups have finite-index subgroups with isomorphic profinite completions.
* An isomorphism of profinite completions of such lattices identifies their finite local fields and their local spin groups, up to permutation. In particular, it preserves the product of the finite local Hasse invariants of the determinant-normalized quadratic forms.

These statements apply here, including to the product of \(r\ge2\) real-rank-one factors.

### The parity obstruction

In odd dimension \(2n+1\), scaling a quadratic form does not change its spin group. We may therefore normalize its determinant to be \(1\) modulo squares.

At a noncompact real place, the determinant-normalized signatures for the two groups are
\[
(2n-1,2),\qquad (1,2n),
\]
respectively. At a compact real place the normalized form is positive definite.

For a real quadratic form with \(s\) negative directions, its Hasse invariant is
\[
(-1)^{s(s-1)/2}.
\]
Thus the respective Hasse invariants at each noncompact real place are
\[
-1,\qquad (-1)^n,
\]
and those at compact real places are \(1\).

Suppose the required lattices exist. Finite-local rigidity identifies the products of their finite Hasse invariants. Applying Hilbert reciprocity to their defining forms therefore gives
\[
(-1)^r=(-1)^{nr},
\]
or equivalently
\[
r(n-1)\equiv0\pmod2.
\]
In particular, if \(r\) is odd, \(n\) must be odd. Since \(n\ge2\), this gives the lower bounds \(n\ge2\) for even \(r\), and \(n\ge3\) for odd \(r\).

### Construction whenever the parity condition holds

Choose a totally real field \(k\) of degree greater than \(r\). At \(r\) real places prescribe the two signatures above, and at all remaining real places prescribe positive-definite forms.

If \(r(n-1)\) is even, the products of the prescribed real Hasse invariants agree. The local-global classification of quadratic forms consequently supplies determinant-one forms \(Q_1,Q_2\) over \(k\) with these signatures and with
\[
(Q_1)_v\cong(Q_2)_v
\qquad\text{at every finite place }v.
\]
Their definite real places make both forms \(k\)-anisotropic, so their arithmetic lattices are cocompact. Their finite adelic spin groups are isomorphic.

The finite congruence kernels can be removed by passing to finite-index subgroups: choose open subgroups of the profinite completions avoiding those kernels, then pass to a common open subgroup of the identified finite adelic groups. This produces lattices with isomorphic profinite completions. Further common finite-index passage makes them torsion-free. They are irreducible by strong approximation, residually finite by linearity, and finitely presented by cocompactness.

The first lattice is Kähler: its locally symmetric quotient is a compact quotient of a product of Hermitian symmetric domains of type
\[
\operatorname{SO}_0(2n-1,2).
\]
The second is not Kähler, by the harmonic-map obstruction for irreducible cocompact lattices in products of real hyperbolic groups of dimension at least three. Here those dimensions are \(2n\ge4\).

Thus the parity lower bounds are attained.

reply:
The question includes a well-known open problem, so an unconditional closed-form value is not currently known.

For \(k\ge d\), pure \(d\)-dimensional \(k\)-decomposability is equivalent to shellability. Consequently, \(b(d,k)=0\) in this range is equivalent to **Simon’s conjecture**: every shelling of a pure subcomplex of the \(d\)-skeleton of a simplex can be extended to a shelling of the whole skeleton.

The fact that the question only requires each intermediate complex to be shellable does not weaken this obstruction. Indeed, suppose \(\Gamma\) and \(\Gamma\cup2^F\) are pure \(d\)-dimensional shellable complexes. Then
\[
\Gamma\cap2^F
\]
must be pure of dimension \(d-1\). Otherwise, choose a maximal face \(G\) of this intersection with \(|G|<d\). The link of \(G\) in \(\Gamma\cup2^F\) is the disjoint union of the nonempty link in \(\Gamma\) and the simplex on \(F\setminus G\). It is disconnected and has positive dimension, contradicting shellability. Thus \(F\) can be appended to any shelling of \(\Gamma\).

Hence an ordering as in the question with no auxiliary vertices gives an actual shelling extension, and conversely any shelling extension supplies such an ordering. Requiring the initial complex to use its entire stated vertex set does not remove the open problem: omitted vertices can be incorporated after completing the skeleton on the vertices already used.

Therefore, already for \(k=d\), determining whether the answer is zero requires resolving Simon’s conjecture, which remains open in general for \(d\ge3\).

This question includes a longstanding open problem: **Simon’s conjecture on extendable shellability of simplex skeleta**.

Indeed, take \(k\ge d\). A pure \(d\)-dimensional complex is \(k\)-decomposable exactly when it is shellable. One direction follows by recursively combining shellings of the deletion and link. Conversely, the restriction face of the last facet in a shelling is a shedding face; deleting it removes precisely that last facet’s new faces.

Consequently, \(b(d,k)=0\) for \(k\ge d\) is equivalent to saying that every shellable pure \(d\)-complex can be completed, by successively adding facets, to the \(d\)-skeleton of the simplex on its existing vertices. This is precisely the shelling-completability formulation of Simon’s conjecture.

We recall the relevant elementary extension argument. Restrict an adjacency matrix to its walk space, writing the resulting symmetric matrix as \(M\), with cyclic vector \(z\).

For a cone, the new matrix and all-ones vector are
\[
\begin{pmatrix}M&z\\z^T&0\end{pmatrix},
\qquad \binom z1.
\]
An eigenvector orthogonal to this new vector can occur only at eigenvalue \(-1\). Consequently:
* if \(-1\) is a simple main eigenvalue of \(M\), coning increases the walk rank by one and removes that eigenvalue;
* if \(M+I\) is nonsingular, coning increases the walk rank by one unless
  \(z^T(M+I)^{-1}z=1\).

Adding an isolated vertex first increases the walk rank by one whenever \(M\) is nonsingular. Schur complements now show that \(T\) increases the walk rank by two in either of these cases:
\[
\begin{cases}
M\text{ nonsingular and }-1\text{ a simple main eigenvalue};\\
M,\ M+I\text{ nonsingular and }z^T(M+I)^{-1}z\ne0.
\end{cases}
\]
Afterward both restricted matrices are nonsingular, and the new value of
\(z^T(M+I)^{-1}z\) is \(1\).

In our base pair, the two-dimensional orthogonal complement of the walk space has adjacency eigenvalues \(\pm\sqrt5\). Thus (1) supplies the first case above. Also, coning the base pair gives walk rank \(9\), with neither \(0\) nor \(-1\) a main eigenvalue, by (1). Hence
\[
T^k(G),T^k(H)\quad(n=10+2k),
\]
and
\[
T^k(C(G)),T^k(C(H))\quad(n=11+2k)
\]
have walk rank \(n-2\).

Literal equality of walk matrices is preserved by both operations, directly from the block multiplication formulas. Connectedness is immediate. \begin{gathered}
x^2=y^2=z^2=0,\qquad xe=ye=ze=xf=yf=zf=0,\\
f^2=e^2,\qquad yg=zg=0,\qquad eg=fg=xg,\\
g^2=-yz-e^2-ef-3xg.
\end{gathered}                                                    \tag{1}
\]
The orientation is normalized by \(xyz=e^3=ef^2=1\).

Here are the two bundle classes in this notation:
\[
u=x-y+z-2e-2f-g,\qquad
v=-x-y+z+f+2g.
\]
In particular, (1) gives
\[
uv=0.
\]
Consequently both projective-bundle rings have the presentation
\[
R=H^*(B;\mathbb Z)[t]/(t^2-qt),\qquad
q=u+v=-2y+2z-2e-f+g.                                  \tag{2}
\]
This equality of presentations does **not** imply that the projective bundles are homotopy equivalent.

We describe the algebraic count first. The primitive square-zero elements of degree two in \(R\) lie on precisely the three lines generated by \(x,y,z\). Their annihilators distinguish the \(x\)-line from the other two. Applying (1) then shows that every automorphism preserves the base subring, and its restriction has the form
\[
(x,e,f,g)\longmapsto\alpha(x,e,f,g),\qquad
(y,z)\longmapsto\beta(y,z)\ \text{or}\ \beta(z,y),
\quad \alpha,\beta\in\{1,-1\}.                         \tag{3}
\]
Thus there are eight possible restrictions.

For each restriction \(A\), the two extensions are
\[
t\longmapsto \varepsilon t+\frac{Aq-\varepsilon q}{2},
\qquad \varepsilon=\pm1.
\]
Indeed, \(Aq\equiv q\pmod2\) and
\[
A(q^2)=q^2=4e^2+3ef-9yz-9xg.
\]
It follows that \(N_{\mathrm{alg}}=16\).

For completeness, the unstable obstruction is essential in counting realizations. In the cellular obstruction calculation for these projective bundles, after fixing the degree-two generators, the remaining obstruction is the \(\mathbb Z/2\)-valued rank-two bundle obstruction on the top cell of \(B\). Its values are
\[
\begin{array}{c|c}
\text{bundle, up to tensoring by a line bundle}&
\text{top-cell obstruction}\\ \hline
\mathcal O\oplus L_q&0\\
L_u\oplus L_v&1 .
\end{array}                                                     \tag{4}
\]
Here the obstruction is genuinely retained: its indeterminacy is the image of
\[
Sq^2+\bar q:H^4(B;\mathbb F_2)\longrightarrow H^6(B;\mathbb F_2),
\]
which is zero because \(w_2(B)=\bar q=\bar f+\bar g\). The calculation in (4) uses the relations (1); all eight changes of generators (3), as well as the two choices of fiber generator, leave this obstruction unchanged.

A map inducing one of the sixteen ring isomorphisms would have degree \(1\) or \(-1\), and naturality of the top-cell obstruction would therefore identify the two entries in (4). Since they differ, no such map exists. Hence none of the algebraic isomorphisms is realizable.

\[
\boxed{(N_{\mathrm{alg}},N_{\mathrm{real}})=(16,0)}
\]

Write \(a=D_2,\ b=D_4,\ c=D_6,\ e=D_7+D_8,\ f=D_8,\ g=D_9\), and put \(s=u+v\). The intersection form of \(B\) is
\[
\int_B(Aa+Bb+Cc+Ee+Ff+Gg)^3
=6ABC+E^3+3EF^2+3G^3-3(A+E+F)G^2.
\tag{1}
\]
In particular, direct multiplication gives \(uv=0\). Thus both projective bundles have the same abstract presentation
\[
H^*(B;\mathbb Z)[t]/(t^2-st),
\tag{2}
\]
where \(t\) is the first Chern class of the tautological line bundle.

Here are the ring-automorphism and realization calculations, including the secondary obstruction relevant to this example.

**Ring isomorphisms.** The only primitive square-zero classes in degree two are
\(\pm a,\pm b,\pm c\). Moreover, multiplication by \(a\) has rank three, whereas multiplication by \(b\) or \(c\) has rank two. The base subring in (2) is intrinsically determined: its degree-two part is the kernel of multiplication by \(abc\).

Using (1), its possible automorphisms are exactly
\[
a\longmapsto\alpha a,\qquad
(b,c)\longmapsto\beta(b,c)\ \text{or }\beta(c,b),\qquad
(e,f,g)\longmapsto\alpha(e,f,g),
\tag{3}
\]
with \(\alpha,\beta\in\{\pm1\}\). There are eight.

For each such automorphism \(\phi\), an extension to (2) necessarily has
\[
t\longmapsto \varepsilon t+\frac{\phi(s)-\varepsilon s}{2},
\qquad \varepsilon=\pm1.
\tag{4}
\]
All sixteen choices work: \(\phi(s)\equiv s\pmod2\) and
\(\phi(s)^2=s^2\). Consequently \(N_{\mathrm{alg}}=16\).

**Realization obstruction.** We use the standard secondary section obstruction for a split rank-two bundle on a simply connected six-manifold with torsion-free cohomology concentrated in even degrees. If
\[
r(q-r)=0,\qquad q\equiv w_2(B)\pmod2,
\]
then the obstruction to
\[
L_r\oplus L_{q-r}\cong\mathcal O\oplus L_q
\]
is the mod-two index
\[
\frac{\langle r^3-rp_1(B),[B]\rangle}{24}\pmod2.
\tag{5}
\]
Equivalently, this is the secondary obstruction to a nowhere-zero section; the displayed quotient is integral under these hypotheses.

In our case,
\[
w_2(B)\equiv s\equiv f+g\pmod2,\qquad
p_1(B)=4e^2+3f^2+3g^2+4eg+2fg.
\]
Formula (1) gives
\[
\int_Bu^3=-32,\qquad \int_Bup_1(B)=-8,
\]
so (5) for \(r=u\) is \(-1\), hence nonzero. The same obstruction is nonzero for \(r=v,-u,-v\).

To apply this to maps not preserving the projections, suppose a map \(h:Y\to X\) induced one of (4). Restrict it to the canonical section \(B\to Y\) whose tautological class is zero. If
\[
d=\frac{\phi(s)-\varepsilon s}{2},
\]
the resulting map to \(X\) supplies a line subbundle \(L_d\) of
\(L_{\phi(u)}\oplus L_{\phi(v)}\). After twisting by \(L_{-d}\), this would give a nowhere-zero section of
\[
L_r\oplus L_{\varepsilon s-r},
\qquad r=\phi(u)-d.
\]
From (3), \(r\) is respectively \(u,v,-v\), or \(-u\). In every case (5) is nonzero—a contradiction. Thus none of the sixteen ring isomorphisms is induced by a continuous map.

\[
\boxed{(N_{\mathrm{alg}},N_{\mathrm{real}})=(16,0)}
\]

We use the **Baer splitting theorem for Boolean powers of a PID**: if \(D\) is a PID that is not a field and \(X\) is a compact Boolean space, then every Baer module over the ring \(C(X,D)\) of locally constant \(D\)-valued functions is projective. Here torsion is defined using the regular elements, and the theorem applies to modules of arbitrary cardinality.

Let \(X=\mathbb N\cup\{\infty\}\) be the one-point compactification of the discrete space \(\mathbb N\). A locally constant map \(X\to\mathbb Z\) is precisely an eventually constant integer sequence. Thus
\[
R=C(X,\mathbb Z),
\]
so the splitting theorem gives \(\beta(R)=0\).

We compute the other entry directly. An element of \(R\) is regular exactly when none of its coordinates is zero. Consequently,
\[
Q=C(X,\mathbb Q),
\]
the ring of eventually constant rational sequences: denominators of such a sequence can be cleared by an eventually constant sequence of nonzero integers.

Every regular element of \(Q\) is a unit. Hence the only regular-torsion \(Q\)-module is zero, and **every \(Q\)-module is Baer**. Therefore \(\beta(Q)=\operatorname{gl.dim}Q\).

Write \(e_n\) for the characteristic function of \(\{n\}\), and put
\[
J=\bigoplus_{n\ge1}\mathbb Qe_n.
\]
Every ideal \(I\subseteq Q\) is projective:

* If \(I\subseteq J\), then \(I\) is a direct sum of some of the ideals \(Qe_n\).
* Otherwise, \(I\) contains an element with nonzero eventual value. Multiplying by its coordinatewise inverse on its support shows that \(I\) contains a cofinite-support idempotent \(e\). Thus
  \[
  I=eQ\oplus(1-e)I,
  \]
  where the second summand is an ideal in a finite product of fields.

Thus \(Q\) is hereditary, so its global dimension is at most \(1\). It is not \(0\): the sequence
\[
0\longrightarrow J\longrightarrow Q\longrightarrow Q/J\longrightarrow0
\]
does not split. Indeed, splitting would make \(J\) an idempotent-generated ideal, whereas no single eventually constant idempotent generates precisely the finitely supported sequences. Hence \(\operatorname{pd}_Q(Q/J)=1\).

\[
\boxed{(\beta(R),\beta(Q))=(0,1)}
\]

We use the Baer splitting theorem in the following form: if \(X\) is a compact Boolean space, then every Baer module over the ring \(C(X,\mathbb Z)\) of continuous integer-valued functions is projective. Here torsion means torsion with respect to the regular elements, and the theorem applies to modules of arbitrary cardinality.

Let \(X=\mathbb N\cup\{\infty\}\) be the one-point compactification of the discrete space \(\mathbb N\). A continuous map \(X\to\mathbb Z\) is precisely an eventually constant integer sequence, with its eventual value assigned to \(\infty\). Consequently,
\[
R\cong C(X,\mathbb Z).
\]
The splitting theorem therefore gives \(\beta(R)=0\).

We compute the other invariant directly. An element of \(R\) is regular exactly when all its coordinates are nonzero: a zero coordinate is detected by the corresponding coordinate idempotent, and the converse follows coordinatewise. Thus
\[
Q\cong C(X,\mathbb Q),
\]
the ring of eventually constant rational sequences. Indeed, any such sequence has a common integer denominator.

The ring \(Q\) is von Neumann regular: for \(a=(a_n)\), take \(b_n=a_n^{-1}\) when \(a_n\ne0\), and \(b_n=0\) otherwise. This is again eventually constant and satisfies \(a^2b=a\). In particular, every regular element of \(Q\) is a unit. Hence its only regular-torsion module is zero, so **every \(Q\)-module is Baer**.

To determine their projective dimensions, write \(e_n\) for the \(n\)-th coordinate idempotent and
\[
J=\bigoplus_{n\ge1}Qe_n.
\]
Every ideal contained in \(J\) is a direct sum of some of the simple projective ideals \(Qe_n\). An ideal not contained in \(J\) contains an element with nonzero eventual value, hence contains a cofinite-support idempotent \(e\). It is then the direct sum of \(Qe\) and an ideal supported on the finite complement. Thus every ideal of \(Q\) is projective. The ideal criterion for hereditary rings gives
\[
\operatorname{gl.dim}Q\le1.
\]

Finally, \(Q/J\) is not projective. Otherwise \(J\) would be a direct-summand ideal, hence generated by an idempotent; but no single finitely supported idempotent generates all of \(J\). Therefore \(\operatorname{pd}_Q(Q/J)=1\), and \(\beta(Q)=1\).

\[
\boxed{(\beta(R),\beta(Q))=(0,1)}
\]

We use the Baer splitting theorem in its almost-Dedekind-ring form: **if a commutative ring is semihereditary and its localization at every maximal ideal is a discrete valuation domain (not a field), then every Baer module is projective.** This theorem applies to modules of arbitrary cardinality; restricting it to countably generated modules would not suffice here.

Put \(e_n=(0,\ldots,0,1,0,\ldots)\). The maximal ideals of \(R\) are
\[
\mathfrak m_{n,p}=\{a:p\mid a_n\},
\qquad
\mathfrak m_{\infty,p}=\{a:p\mid a_\infty\},
\]
where \(p\) is prime and \(a_\infty\) denotes the eventual value. In both cases the localization is \(\mathbb Z_{(p)}\): at \(\mathfrak m_{n,p}\), the idempotent \(e_n\) becomes \(1\), while at \(\mathfrak m_{\infty,p}\), every \(e_n\) becomes \(0\).

Moreover, \(R\) is semihereditary. Indeed, for finitely many generators of an ideal, choose a common tail on which they are constant. The corresponding finite idempotent decomposition reduces that ideal to finitely many principal ideals of \(\mathbb Z\) and one principal ideal on the tail; each is projective. Thus the quoted splitting theorem gives
\[
\beta(R)=0.
\]

A sequence in \(R\) is regular precisely when all its coordinates are nonzero. Consequently,
\[
Q\cong\{(q_n)\in\mathbb Q^{\mathbb N}:q_n\text{ is eventually constant}\}.
\]
This is a von Neumann regular ring, so its regular elements are units. Its only regular-torsion module is therefore \(0\), and **every \(Q\)-module is Baer**.

To compute its global dimension, let
\[
J=\bigoplus_{n\ge1}Qe_n.
\]
Every ideal contained in \(J\) is a direct sum of coordinate ideals and hence projective. Any other ideal contains an idempotent which is \(1\) on a tail; splitting off that tail again shows that the ideal is projective. Thus \(Q\) is hereditary.

Finally, \(Q/J\) is not projective. Otherwise \(J\) would be an idempotent-generated direct summand of \(Q\), impossible because no eventually constant idempotent has support equal to all of \(\mathbb N\) while belonging to \(J\). Hence \(\operatorname{pd}_Q(Q/J)=1\), and \(\beta(Q)=1\).

\[
\boxed{(\beta(R),\beta(Q))=(0,1)}
\]
